title: Docker deployment (multi-stage builds, health probes)
hook: Running dotnet run on a developer laptop is not production. Docker packages your ASP.NET Core Web API into a portable image with a known runtime, and Kubernetes or any container platform uses health probes to know when your app is ready to receive traffic and when to restart a failing pod.

blocks.text: A multi-stage Dockerfile builds your app in a SDK image (with compilers) and copies only the published output into a slim ASP.NET runtime image — keeping production images small and secure. Health checks expose /health (liveness: is the process alive?) and /health/ready (readiness: can it serve traffic — database connected?). Kubernetes livenessProbe restarts unhealthy pods; readinessProbe removes pods from load balancer until ready.

entries.plainDefinition: Separate build and runtime stages — SDK image compiles, runtime image runs.
entries.example: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build ... FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0

entries.plainDefinition: Checks if container is alive — failure triggers restart.
Checks if container can accept traffic — failure removes from service endpoints.
Binds Kestrel to container port — typically http://+:8080 for non-root.

blocks.text: Production APIs deploy to Kubernetes, Azure Container Apps, AWS ECS, or GitHub Actions → container registry → GitHub Pages is for static Angular output, not the API itself. Correct Dockerfile and health probes prevent deploys that pass CI but fail in prod — app starts but cannot reach database, or BackgroundService deadlock blocks readiness. Senior interviews ask how you know a pod is healthy beyond 'it started'.

blocks.title: Do not use SDK image in production
blocks.body: Running mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk in production bloats image size (~700MB vs ~200MB), includes compilers attackers could abuse, and violates least-privilege container security.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile
items.body: restore → build → publish in SDK stage; copy publish output to aspnet runtime stage.

items.title: Configure Kestrel
items.body: ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080, run as non-root user in runtime image.

items.title: Register health checks
items.body: AddHealthChecks with EF DbContext check, custom SQS check optional.

items.title: Kubernetes probes
items.body: readinessProbe on /health/ready, livenessProbe on /health/live with appropriate timeouts.

diagram.title: Multi-stage Docker build
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  SRC[Source code] --> SDK[dotnet/sdk stage\nrestore build publish]
  SDK --> OUT[publish output]
  OUT --> RT[dotnet/aspnet stage\ncopy + ENTRYPOINT]
  RT --> IMG[Production image\n~200MB]
  IMG --> K8s[Kubernetes pod\nliveness + readiness]

snippet.label: Multi-stage Dockerfile for Web API
snippet.code:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["OrderApi/OrderApi.csproj", "OrderApi/"]
RUN dotnet restore "OrderApi/OrderApi.csproj"
COPY . .
WORKDIR /src/OrderApi
RUN dotnet publish -c Release -o /app/publish /p:UseAppHost=false

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 AS final
WORKDIR /app
EXPOSE 8080
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
ENV ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production

# Run as non-root (aspnet image includes app user)
USER $APP_UID

COPY --from=build /app/publish .
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "OrderApi.dll"]
snippet.explanation: SDK stage compiles; final stage only has runtime + published DLLs. UseAppHost=false avoids platform-specific apphost. USER $APP_UID runs non-root. Port 8080 is convention for containerized ASP.NET Core.

snippet.label: Health checks — liveness vs readiness
snippet.explanation: Liveness is lightweight — pod restart if process dead. Readiness includes DB and external deps — pod removed from load balancer until ready. Tag-based filtering separates concerns.

snippet.label: Kubernetes deployment probes
snippet.code:
spec:
  containers:
  - name: order-api
    image: ghcr.io/org/order-api:1.2.3
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health/live
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 15
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health/ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "256Mi"
        cpu: "100m"
      limits:
        memory: "512Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
snippet.explanation: Readiness fails when DB migration pending or connection pool exhausted — pod not routed traffic. Liveness fails on deadlock — pod restarted. Set resources to avoid OOMKill during traffic spikes.

snippet.label: Graceful shutdown for BackgroundService
snippet.explanation: Default 5s shutdown may kill BackgroundService mid-batch. Increase ShutdownTimeout and K8s terminationGracePeriodSeconds. PreStop hook gives drain time before pod removal.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Single-stage Dockerfile with SDK in production. Binding to localhost (127.0.0.1) instead of 0.0.0.0/+ in container. Readiness check includes slow external API — all pods marked unready during outage. Liveness check hits database — restart loop when DB down. Forgetting migration strategy — app starts but readiness fails until MigrateAsync runs.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: kubectl describe pod shows readiness probe failures with HTTP status. Application Insights dependency failures correlate with readiness 503 spikes. Image scan (Trivy, Grype) on CI — no critical CVEs in base image. Deploy pipeline: build → test → push to GHCR → rolling update with maxUnavailable 0. dotnet-counters inside container via kubectl exec for threadpool during rollout. PreStop hook + graceful shutdown: verify outbox messages not duplicated on deploy.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Single-stage Dockerfile with SDK in production. Liveness probe checking database — causes restart storm when DB is down. Not knowing difference between liveness and readiness. Unable to explain graceful shutdown for BackgroundService during rolling deploy.

interviewTakeaways: Multi-stage Dockerfile: SDK builds, aspnet runtime runs — smaller, more secure production image.
Liveness = process alive (restart on fail). Readiness = can serve traffic (DB connected) — remove from LB on fail.
Production tip: non-root USER, ASPNETCORE_URLS=:8080, extend ShutdownTimeout for BackgroundService drain.

60s: SDK stage restore build publish. Aspnet stage copy output ENTRYPOINT dotnet. Map /health/live and /health/ready with tag filters. K8s readiness on DB, liveness lightweight. Graceful shutdown with stoppingToken.
Follow-up: how do rolling deploys interact with BackgroundService and outbox duplicate publishes?
commonPitfalls: SDK image in production gets you rejected — always multi-stage with aspnet runtime.
Liveness probe hitting database — restart loop when DB unavailable; readiness should check DB instead.

Strong answer: 'Multi-stage Dockerfile ~200MB aspnet image. Readiness includes DbContextCheck. Liveness is self-check only. terminationGracePeriodSeconds 45 for outbox drain. Trivy scan in CI. NestJS same pattern with node:alpine.'
introducedIn: Docker support since .NET Core 1.0; health checks since ASP.NET Core 2.2

jsTsCorrelations.note: NestJS uses node:20-alpine builder stage (npm ci, nest build) and slim runtime stage — same multi-stage principle. Health endpoint via @nestjs/terminus mirrors MapHealthChecks.
